patient_name: OET role-play — daughter asking whether her dying mother is 'being starved' as she eats less
chief_complaint: In a hospice, respond to a distressed daughter who fears her dying mother is being starved, explain reduced eating at the end of life, and show her how she can help

team_brief.title: End-of-life care: a daughter who asks 'Are you starving her?'
team_brief.patient: Mrs Lucia Herrera, 82-year-old woman with advanced bowel cancer that has spread to the liver, in the last days to weeks of life; the conversation is with her daughter, Ms Mariana Herrera, 54. Mrs Herrera has agreed that her family can be told about her care.
team_brief.location: Hospice inpatient unit; you are the nurse caring for Mrs Herrera today, talking to her daughter in the family room
team_brief.situation: Ms Herrera lives in another city and arrived last night. She has noticed that her mother is eating only a few spoonfuls a day and is asking why she is not being given a drip or a feeding tube. She is upset and asks whether her mother is being starved.
background: Over the past two weeks Mrs Herrera has become weaker and sleeps most of the day. She takes small sips of water and a few spoonfuls of yoghurt or soup when she is awake.
Two weeks ago, when she was more alert, Mrs Herrera told the team that she wanted to be kept comfortable, stay at the hospice, and did not want 'drips or tubes'. This is recorded in her care plan.
Ms Herrera has one brother, who visits daily; she was not present when her mother discussed her wishes.
current_status: Mrs Herrera appears comfortable, with no signs of pain or distress; her mouth is sometimes dry.
She is offered food and drink whenever she is awake and wants it.
key_data: As the body becomes very ill near the end of life, it can no longer use food and fluid in the usual way. Loss of appetite and thirst is a natural part of this process, and people do not usually feel hungry in the way a healthy person would. She is not dying because she is not eating; she is eating less because she is dying.

A drip or feeding tube is unlikely to help her live longer or feel better at this stage, and can cause discomfort, such as swelling, fluid on the chest, or the need for a needle or tube. Decisions are made individually, and the doctor can discuss this further with the family.
She should never be pushed to eat or drink. Food and drink are offered only when she is awake, sitting up and able to swallow, and she can stop whenever she wants.
Dry mouth is the main cause of discomfort and is relieved by regular mouth care, such as moist swabs, lip balm, and small sips when she is awake and able to swallow.
Family can help by offering small tastes of favourite foods or drinks when she is awake and sitting up, doing mouth care, and spending time talking to her or holding her hand.
treatments: Already done: comfort-focused care plan; medicines for symptom control as needed; regular mouth care.
Pending: the doctor is available to meet the family today if they wish.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Ms Herrera's concerns, explain why her mother is eating less and why artificial feeding is not planned, and show her how she can help care for her mother.
must_include: Find out what Ms Herrera has noticed and what she is most worried about.
Acknowledge her distress and respond to her question about starvation with sensitivity.
Explain in plain language why her mother is eating and drinking less near the end of life.
Explain why a drip or feeding tube is not planned, including her mother's own wishes, and offer a meeting with the doctor.
Advise her on practical ways she can help keep her mother comfortable, such as mouth care and small tastes of favourite foods.

kickoff_text: Can I ask you something, and I want an honest answer? My mother has hardly eaten anything since I got here. Are you just... letting her starve?
persona_override: You are Mariana Herrera, a 54-year-old teacher whose mother, Lucia Herrera, 82, is dying of advanced bowel cancer in a hospice. You live in another city and arrived last night after a long drive. You love your mother deeply; in your family, cooking and feeding people is how love is shown, and your mother fed everyone all her life. You are exhausted, shocked by how much she has changed, guilty that you were not here sooner, and angry in a controlled way. Your specific fear: that your mother is hungry and thirsty and the staff are 'giving up' on her by not putting in a drip or feeding tube. Ground truth: you last saw your mother six weeks ago, when she was still cooking; you noticed today she only took two spoonfuls of soup; you saw her lips were dry; your brother visits daily but did not tell you how much she had changed; you do not know that your mother told the team she did not want drips or tubes; you have never been with someone who is dying. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words like 'palliative', 'artificial nutrition and hydration', 'cachexia', 'anorexia', 'subcutaneous fluids' or 'advance care plan' without explaining them, ask what they mean. If the nurse jumps straight to explaining the biology without first acknowledging how upsetting this is, say more sharply: 'I don't need a lecture. I need to know she's not suffering.' If the nurse never directly answers whether your mother is hungry or suffering, ask again, more distressed: 'But is she hungry? Is she thirsty? Just tell me.' If the nurse acknowledges your feelings and explains gently that she is eating less because her body is shutting down, not the other way round, soften and become tearful once. When you hear that your mother said she did not want drips or tubes, go quiet, then say 'She never told me that.' Accept the explanation gradually: first ask 'Wouldn't a drip at least help a bit?', then ask 'So what can I do for her?' Respond warmly to practical suggestions such as mouth care or bringing a favourite food. If the nurse offers a meeting with the doctor, accept it. If the nurse gives false hope (for example, that she might recover if she eats), become confused. Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: thank the nurse, say you would like to help with her mouth care, and ask to see the doctor later today.
learning_objectives: find out what the daughter has noticed and what she is most worried about
acknowledge her distress and answer the question about starvation with sensitivity
explain that her mother is eating less because her body is shutting down, not the other way round
explain why a drip or feeding tube is not planned and her mother's own wishes
advise practical ways to help: mouth care, small tastes of favourite foods, being with her
offer a meeting with the doctor
suggested_questions: That's a really important question, and I'm glad you asked me. Can you tell me what you've noticed since you arrived?

I can see how hard it is to see your mum like this. From what we can see, she doesn't seem hungry or distressed, and she looks comfortable. Her body is slowing down, so it can't use food the way it used to — she's eating less because she's very ill, not the other way round.
A drip or tube at this stage wouldn't help her live longer or feel better, and it can make people more uncomfortable. When she was more awake, your mum also told us she didn't want drips or tubes.
There's a lot you can do for her. Would you like me to show you how to keep her mouth moist, and is there a food or drink she's always loved that we could offer her in small tastes?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Explaining reduced oral intake near the end of life to a distressed relative
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NICE NG31 (care of dying adults in the last days of life) and Marie Curie guidance for families; decisions about clinically assisted nutrition and hydration are individual and follow the treating team, the patient's recorded wishes and local policy
core_concepts: Reduced appetite and thirst are expected in the last days to weeks of life; the underlying illness, not lack of food, is the cause of decline.
Clinically assisted nutrition or hydration near the end of life rarely improves comfort or survival and can cause burdens; decisions are individualised and discussed with patient and family.
Relatives often experience a loved one's refusal of food as abandonment or starvation, especially where food carries cultural meaning; this distress must be acknowledged.
diagnostic_clues: A relative who has arrived recently and 'was not told' may be experiencing shock and guilt as well as fear.
Direct questions like 'Is she suffering?' need a direct, honest answer before any explanation.
common_misconceptions: A dying person who is not eating is starving and feeling hunger.
A drip will always make a dying person more comfortable or help them live longer.
Offering food should stop once someone is at the end of life.
dangerous_errors: Forcing or encouraging feeding when the patient is drowsy or not sitting up, which risks choking.
Dismissing the relative's concern or implying she is wrong to ask.
Giving false hope that eating more would lead to recovery, or stating a precise time until death.
management_principles: Acknowledge emotion and answer the direct question honestly and gently.
Explain the natural process in simple language, include the patient's own wishes, and avoid false hope.
Offer the relative a meaningful role in comfort care and a meeting with the doctor.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Whether clinically assisted hydration is offered or trialled is an individual clinical decision, varies between settings and countries, and should be discussed with the doctor.
The patient's recorded wishes and capacity, and consent to share information with family, follow local law and policy.
If the patient shows signs of distress, thirst or discomfort, the team should reassess symptom management promptly.
